To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in the early stages of infiltration by leukemic cells, the cells adhere to endothelial cells, and gaps form in the endothelial lining; in the late stages, the cells migrate back into the sinusoid through pores in the endothelal lining.
the sinusoidal endothelial cell is a barrier to invasion by leukemic cells and that the endothelium may be disrupted in several ways.
in early stages of liver infiltration by leukemic cells, leukemia cells pass through the gaps in the sinusoidal endothelium, whereas in later stages, they pass through pores within endothelial cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which leukemia cells invade the liver and with the mechanisms by means of which the sinusoidal wall responds to the invasion of the leukemic cells.
the mechanisms of leukocyte migration into and out of the liver sinusoids.
the mechanism of invasion of the liver by leukemic myeocytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
leukemia cells invade the liver sinusoids of RF mice by a variety of methods.

leukemia cells invade the liver sinusoids of RF mice by passing through gaps in the endothelial cells, by passing through the endothelium of occluded sinusoids, and by passing through pores in the endothelial cells.

the sinusoidal wall is the primary barrier to the passage of leukemic myelocyte cells into the extravascular space, and that the leukemic cell can enter the extravascular tissue by one of two mechanisms: 1) the leukemic cell passes through a gap in the endothelilium or 2) the endothelium is disrupted, the leukemic cells enter the extravascular area, and then migrate back into the sinusoid through temporary pores in endothelial cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
leukemia cells invaded sinusoids of mouse liver by passing through the endothelial cells, and by occluding the sinusoids.
leukemic myelocytic cells invade the liver sinusoid in two ways.
the liver sinusoidal endothelium of RF mice during leukemia invasion is a dynamic structure that changes in appearance in response to the leukemic myelocyte invasion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sinusoids of the liver are an important site for invasion by leukemia cells.
the endothelium of the sinusoids of the liver is not always continuous, but rather may be discontinuous or even absent, and that leukemic cells can invade the extravascular space through these gaps.
the endothelial cells are the primary target of leukemic cells.
